analytic.title: Memory Servers for Multicore Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In multicore systems, tasks can be significantly delayed due to contention for access to shared physical resources. Due to the complexity of the underlying hardware arbitration, analyzing resources such as DRAM main memory is challenging. In particular, compositional delay bounds tend to be highly pessimistic, while non-compositional bounds are tighter but prevent independent subsystem development. To address this issue, in this paper we introduce a novel memory server for multicore real-time systems under partitioned fixed-priority scheduling. Similar to a hierarchical server, our memory server regulates the amount of resource (bandwidth) that a group of tasks is allowed to consume, but the server interface is modified to account for the properties of delay analysis. We show how to derive schedulability conditions for each server and for the system as a whole. Our technique can support multiple memory regulation implementations and delay analyses, while significantly improving system schedulability compared to the unregulated case.

div.head: II. DRAM BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
div.p: Since we focus on applying our technique to DRAM main memory, we start by discussing related work on DRAM memory management for real-time systems in Section II-A. We then provide additional details on bandwidth regulation and DRAM delay analysis in Sections II-B and II-C.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In multicore systems, tasks can be significantly delayed due to contention for access to shared physical resources such as caches, interconnections and main memory. In memory intensive systems, DRAM main memory is often the main bottleneck [35], [40]. For this reason, a significant amount of effort has been devoted to analyze and control the impact of memory sharing. One way to address the problem is adopting real-time DRAM controllers [22], [1], [9], [25], [7], [34], [17], which offer certain timing guarantees in accessing DRAM by hardware design. However, such hardware approaches are not available on COTS systems.

In analyzing existing main memory systems, many works rely on several common assumptions such as round-robin arbitration and a single resource model [27], [29], [28]. While these assumptions make analysis simpler, they are not generally applicable to COTS memory systems. Concretely, COTS DRAM controllers typically implement a FR-FCFS scheduling algorithm [26], which re-orders requests to maximize throughput, and can further support architectural optimizations such as write buffering and read prioritization to hide write processing delays in the critical path [19], [10]. Recently, more realistic delay analyses have been introduced in the literature [16], [38]. These analyses derive both a request driven delay bound, which is independent of the activity of other cores, as well as a job driven bound, which requires knowledge of tasks running on all cores. Unfortunately, request driven bounds can be highly pessimistic, limiting their usefulness especially for memory intensive applications. Job driven bounds are tighter, This work is supported in part by NSERC DG 402369-2011 and NSF CNS 1302563. Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this publication are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the sponsors. but they cannot be applied to partitioned and component-based systems where subsystems running on one core do not have detailed knowledge of computation running on other cores (i.e., job driven analysis is non-compositional).

Motivated by such advances in resource delay analysis and to allow compositional system development, the main contribution of this paper is a novel memory server for multicore real-time systems using partitioned fixed-priority scheduling. Similar to a hierarchical server [32], our server regulates the amount of resource (memory bandwidth) that a group of tasks is allowed to consume. In this way, each core can be analyzed in isolation to derive a server interface: the analysis guarantees that all tasks on the core are feasible if the allocation of resources satisfies the requirements in the interface. A systemlevel analysis can then be used to ensure that all interfaces can be simultaneously satisfied. By abstracting the characteristics of the tasks running on a core into a simplified interface, we argue that this approach enables independent subsystem development on each core.

More in details, we first discuss how to realize the server abstraction for DRAM main memory based on available memory regulation mechanisms. We then show how to model the server interface. Compared to classic hierarchical servers, the key novelty in our approach is that the system utilization (bandwidth) bound is different for each task; this is a consequence of applying the job driven analysis. Despite this, the complexity of deriving the interface is comparable to standard schedulability analysis for fixed-priority uniprocessor systems. We also show that based on the derived interfaces, a necessary and sufficient system-level analysis is possible. Finally, our evaluation demonstrates that our memory server-based analysis schemes can significantly improve system schedulability compared to other compositional analyses.

The remaining sections are organized as follows: Section II discusses related work and required background. Section III introduces the system model and our memory server, while Sections IV and V provide detailed schedulability analysis. Section VI evaluates our memory server solution. Finally, we conclude in Section VII. the overall performance. Therefore, there has been significant effort in the real-time research community to understand and analyze its behavior. The complexities of COTS DRAM systems, however, have made such effort difficult. Therefore, many researchers have chosen to design real-time DRAM controllers [22], [1], [9], [25], [7], [34], [17] that are easier to analyze and offer certain performance guarantees (e.g., latency and bandwidth). Unfortunately, these real-time DRAM controllers are not designed to offer higher average performancemost important design goal for COTS systems-and are not available in COTS systems. Therefore, there is a greater demand to better understand and analyze COTS memory systems, especially from industry practitioners. One way to deal with COTS memory systems is measurement based approaches. The WCET of a task is estimated through measurements in the presence of "stress benchmarks" running on the other cores [24], [20]. The problem of this approach is that there is no guarantee that measured execution times are indeed the worst-case. Another, more analytic approach is to make certain assumptions about the inner working of the considered COTS memory system and build a system model and its analysis method. As always, the validity of such analysis directly depends on the validity of the assumptions they build up on. Initially, commonly adopted assumptions view the main memory as a single resource that is arbitrated by a well-known scheduling algorithm such as round-robin, FIFO, or TDMA [27], [29], [28]. Unfortunately, such simplistic assumptions do not match with the reality of complex COTS memory systems: first of all, modern DRAM is composed of multiple resources called banks that can be accessed in parallel; second, COTS memory controllers typically implement variations of FR-FCFS scheduling algorithm [26] that re-order requests to maximize memory throughput. More recently, Kim et al. proposed a more realistic analysis that considers FR-FCFS [16]. The work in [38] extends the analysis to handle multiple outstanding requests for each competing core and to cover additional write-buffering and read prioritization features. We review delay analysis for FR-FCFS controllers in more details in Section II-C.

To obtain less pessimistic bounds, the use of memory bandwidth regulation mechanisms (sometimes called "throttling" mechanisms) has been recently explored [39], [36], [18], [21]. Memory bandwidth regulation was first introduced in [3] and has been recently improved upon and adopted in modern multicore systems [39], [40], [13]. The basic idea is to limit the maximum amount of memory accesses that a core can generate for a given duration of time; since our proposed solution also relies on memory regulation, we detail the MemGuard management system in Section II-B. Memory bandwidth regulation enables the possibility of compositional analysis, which does not require information of other cores. Based on this concept, several analysis methods have been proposed [39], [36], [18], [21]. Unfortunately, such regulationbased analyses assume simple memory models, such as roundrobin or FIFO scheduling, that are not compatible with FR-FCFS memory controllers. In contrast, our work is based on a FR-FCFS memory model and applies bandwidth regulation to find compositional WCET bounds for partitioned systems. Recently, an analysis based on FR-FCFS [12] has been proposed for the Multi-Resource Server introduced in [21]. However, the analysis is based on more pessimistic request driven bounds only, and does not provide an algorithmic way to assign server parameters.

div.head: B. Memory Bandwidth Regulation
div.p: MemGuard is a memory bandwidth management system, implemented at the OS layer, which can control the performance impact of bandwidth sharing [40]. Its most basic functionality is memory bandwidth regulation, which sets a firm limit on how much memory bandwidth is allowed for each core. It works periodically, and for each time interval, e.g., 1ms, a user-defined memory budget is given to each core. In each core, it uses a hardware performance counter (PMC) to monitor the amount of memory traffic generated by the core. The PMC is programmed to generate an overflow interrupt if the traffic reaches the core's given budget. When the overflow interrupt occurs, MemGuard stalls the core by scheduling a high priority real-time idle thread until the next period begins. Otherwise, the core continues to execute without any interruption. At the beginning of the next period, the process repeats. No hardware support is required outside of PMC. While MemGuard also supports bandwidth reclaiming and sharing features for better average resource utilization (details can be found in [40]), we do not consider such features in this paper as they do not affect worst-case performance.

div.head: C. FR-FCFS Delay Analysis
div.p: We next briefly summarize the major results on delay analysis for FR-FCFS memory controllers as discussed in [16], [38]. While we base the discussion in this section on our previous work [38], as we argue in Section IV and demonstrate in Appendix, our server solution can also be applied to the analysis by Kim et al. [16]. More in general, the fundamental assumption in our method is the availability of a delay analysis that bounds the maximum amount of inter-core interference based on the number of requests performed by each core; hence, we believe that the method could be likely extended to cover other, future analyses deriving job driven delay bounds for physical resources. In this sense, we would like to stress that, despite being to the best of our knowledge the current state of the art, both analyses in [16], [38] have significant limitations. For example, they do not consider delay due to related cache effects such as contention for the Miss Status Hold Register (MSHR) required to handle outstanding requests to main memory [33]. Furthermore, each analysis is necessarily based on a specific controller model, which is difficult to validate since hardware vendors do not typically release information on the detailed implementation of the memory controller.

The analysis in [38] considers a modern out-of-order multicore architecture with a shared DRAM. Each core can generate multiple outstanding memory requests at a time. Last Level Cache (LLC) is non-blocking and can handle multiple concurrent outstanding requests. The DRAM subsystem is composed of a single-channel DRAM controller and a DDR memory module. The DRAM controller uses a FR-FCFS scheduling algorithm [26], which first prioritizes row-hit requests, over row-miss ones, and then older requests over younger ones. The controller has a separate read and a write request buffer and processes writes opportunistically, following the high/low watermark scheme [19], [6] 1 . To obtain meaningful bounds, the analysis further assumes that DRAM banks are partitioned among the cores, which has been shown to be feasible in COTS systems [16], [37].

Given this system model, the analysis provides two ways to compute memory interference delays: request driven and job driven analysis. DRAM-related notation used throughout this section and the rest of the paper is summarized in Table I. DRAM Model symbols represent parameters of the platform; in particular, relevant timing parameters (tBU RST, tRRD, tF AW and tRC) are expressed in number of memory cycles and based on the same LPDDR2 533Mhz memory used in [38], albeit the analysis is applicable to any DDR memory 2 . DRAM computer parameters are derived either in [38] (tM AX, L W , N B ) or in Section IV-B and are used to simplify notation; we explain their role where they are first introduced in the paper. Request driven analysis: In the request driven analysis, the worst-case delay of a task under analysis is expressed as a function of number of read requests of the task. If a task τ i generates H R i read requests, its request driven worst-case delay can be obtained as H R i •RD where RD is the worst-case interference delay of a single memory read request, which is expressed as:
div.formula: RD = L(N rq ) + N B • L W . (1
div.p: Note that L(N rq ) represents the delay caused by competing N rq read requests and N B • L W represents the delay caused by N B batches of write requests. It is important to note that the number of competing read requests N rq can be much larger than the number of competing cores, as each competing core can generate multiple outstanding requests at a time; this is a key difference compared to round-robin arbitration [36], [18], which limites the number of competing requests to one per core. In computing L(N rq ), the analysis takes overlapped request processing capabilities of modern DRAM controllers into account to minimize pessimism, resulting in the following equation (see Theorem 6 in [38]):

Although write-buffering improves average performance by removing write processing in the task's critical path, in the worst-case, each read request under analysis can be delayed by batches of write requests that must be drained according to the wartermark scheme. When the number of writes per batch is N wd , the number of write batches N B and the batch processing time L W are given as follows (Equation 6-7 of [38]):

div.p: Job driven analysis: Unlike the request driven analysis, which makes no assumption on the behavior of the competing cores, the job driven analysis requires the knowledge of the amount of memory traffic generated by the contending cores over the duration of the analyzed task's execution time. Job-driven analysis results in lower delay bounds when the task under analysis is highly memory intensive while the other tasks on contending cores are not (especially when the number of contending writes is small). div.p: III. MEMORY SERVER Based on the discussion in Section II, we now detail our main contribution: the design of a novel server to improve resource bandwidth utilization in partitioned multicore systems. We first introduce the task and regulation model in Section III-A, then detail the analysis strategy in Section III-B.

div.head: A. System Model
div.p: We consider a multicore system comprising M homogeneous cores and a single DRAM main memory. A set of realtime tasks is statically partitioned among the M cores; for core p, we let N p be the number of tasks {τ 1,p , . . . , τ Np,p } assigned to the core. Each task τ i,p is defined by a tuple of parameters:
div.formula: {C i,p , T i,p , D i,p , H R i,p , H W i,p }. C i,p
div.p: represents the execution time of the task when running in isolation, i.e., without suffering memory interference from other cores or being stalled by the regulation mechanism. T i,p , D i,p represent the task's period and deadline. We assume constrained deadlines, i.e., D i,p ≤ T i,p for every task. All times are integer values.
Finally, H R i,p and H W i,p represent the maximum number of read and write requests to main memory, respectively, generated during the execution of the task.

We assume that on each core, tasks are scheduled according to preemptive fixed priority; without loss of generality, tasks within a core are indexed by decreasing priority. To simplify the exposition of the analysis, we assume that all overheads of preemption are already included in the tasks' parameters. For cache-based systems, we assume that Cache-Related Preemption Delay (CRPD) analysis [11], [2] is employed to obtain bounds on the number of cache evictions, and thus additional memory accesses, suffered by each task; these additional accesses, and their associated latency assuming no interference from other cores, must be incorporated in H R i,p , H W i,p and C i,p . Note that the core-local schedulability analysis in Section IV could also be easily modified to incorporate CRPD delay at the busy interval-level rather than task-level, should the employed CRPD analysis provide tighter interval-level bounds. Similarly, we do not include the overhead of running the PMC monitoring code, which was estimated at around 1% of processor utilization in [40], in the analysis. Finally, again for simplicity we do not consider task blocking due to shared resources outside of main memory, but since our schedulability analysis uses the technique introduced in [4] which supports shared resources, it could also easily be extended in this sense.

It is important to note that in the rest of the paper, we only consider delay due to main memory and ignore all other sources of contention between cores. While we recognize that such assumption is generally not true of COTS platforms, we do so for simplicity, and because to our understanding no comprehensive analysis exists yet that can handle all physical resources in a COTS system. As argued in [5], we believe that all contention sources (which for a given platform might include, but not limited to, the interconnection, shared cache allocation, cache ports, MSHR, etc.) should either be mitigated using suitable software solutions such that their effect becomes negligible, or the associated delay should be included in the analysis. For example, if the system employs a shared LLC, then LLC can be statically partitioned among cores to prevent inter-core allocation interference.

Accesses to main memory are regulated based on Mem-Guard. Each regulation interval has a constant length of time P and starts synchronously on all cores. Each core p is assigned a regulation budget Q p in number of memory accesses; as in Section II-B, once tasks executing on core p generate Q p requests in a regulation interval, the currently running task is immediately de-scheduled (the core is stalled) until the beginning of the next interval. We consider two different types of regulation, based on the type of monitored memory accesses and available PMCs: 3 1) the budget Q p is used for read requests only and write requests are not regulated; 2) regulation is based on the sum of read and write requests 3 For example, a LLC miss counter in Intel processors [40], [14] can be used for Read Regulation while a system bus transaction counter in Freescale e500mc processor [8] can be used for Read/Write Regulation.

div.head: B. Server Interface and Analysis
div.p: Our memory server is inspired by the standard framework and motivation for hierarchical scheduling [32]. Under hierarchical scheduling, the system is composed of a set of components, each comprising multiple tasks or subcomponents. Each component is independently developed; hence, the designer of one component is not privy to the detailed characteristics of tasks executing in an unrelated component. Schedulability analysis can then be performed in two steps. First, a component-local analysis is carried out to derive a component's server interface, typically expressed as an amount of budget Q and period P ; the analysis guarantees that all tasks within the component are schedulable if the component receives at least Q units of resource every P time units. Then, a system-level analysis is used to guarantee that the requirements of all top-level components can be satisfied based on their interfaces only. Similarly in our system, tasks executed on a given core p form a subsystem, or software partition, that is independent of all other cores. We find this to be a highly desirable assumption for future safety-critical multicore systems, especially in the aerospace domain [30]. For each core p, our core-level analysis in Section IV computes the interface for the memory server (regulation mechanism) on that core; the analysis guarantees that all tasks on p are schedulable if the allocation of bandwidth, based on the memory regulation budgets Q p , satisfies the requirements of the interface. The system-level analysis in Section V then tests whether the interfaces of all M cores can be simultaneously satisfied.

The key difference between the two approaches lies in the way the server interface is specified. Assuming that the period P is fixed, the only parameter in the interface of a traditional hierarchical server is the required budget Q; in other words, the requirement is a left-closed, right-unbounded interval in N, see Figure 1(a). System-level analysis then checks whether the sum of the utilizations Q/P for all top-level servers is less than or equal to a given utilization bound UB, which depends on the specific scheduling algorithm. Unfortunately, as it will become clear in the next section, this approach does not work for main memory. The key intuition is that we cannot derive a global utilization bound that is not extremely pessimistic; such a bound would force us to use request driven analysis, while our objective is to employ the better job driven delay bounds which require us to limit the amount of requests (A R and A W ) generated by other cores.

Therefore, we instead specify our server interface in terms of two parameters: the minimum amount of memory budget Q p for core p, and the maximum amount of budget QB p (budget bound) that can be assigned to other cores. More precisely, our interface is a subset of N 2 , as shown in the example in Figure 1(b). In the figure, the shaded region represents the schedulability envelope for core p: tasks {τ 1,p , . . . , τ Np,p } are guaranteed to be schedulable for any budget assignment (Q p , QB p ) within the envelope. As we show in Section IV, the schedulability envelope is the union of regions of the form
div.formula: Q p ≥ Q p ∧ QB p ≤ QB p ,
div.p: where Q p and QB p are values computed by the analysis. Note that for some values of Q p , any value of QB p may be acceptable, i.e. the budget bound in unbounded. In this case we set QB p = +∞ to mean that the condition QB p ≤ QB p is always met independently of the budget assigned to other cores; as it will be shown in Sections IV-C, IV-D, this means that we can apply request driven analysis.
As an example 4 , the envelope in Figure 1(b) can be expressed as:

Given a set of M interfaces, the goal of the system-level analysis is then to determine if there exists a budget assignment that falls within the schedulability envelopes of all cores. In Section V we show how to perform a necessary and sufficient test for this problem in reasonable computational complexity.

div.head: IV. CORE-LEVEL ANALYSIS
div.p: We now discuss how to derive the server interface for core p, based only on the knowledge of the parameters of the memory controller and the tasks scheduled on p. We begin by discussing our analysis framework, then detail how to derive the delay due to either memory interference or regulation.

div.head: A. Fixed-Priority Schedulability Analysis

The analysis checks, for each task τ i,p , if there exists a i-level busy interval that finishes before a time instant in S i,p ; in this case, the task is guaranteed to meet its deadline.
We next show how to consider the effects of memory regulation and memory interference on the tasks running on core p. We start with the following observation.
Observation 1: Consider a i-level busy interval for task τ i,p . In the worst case, tasks in the busy interval can be stalled for no more than P time units before starting to execute.

Observation 1 follows immediately by noticing that when the busy interval starts, in the worst case the memory budget might be already exhausted; in this case, the regulation mechanism stalls core p until the beginning of the next regulation interval. Hence, to account for the worst case situation we assume that the core is stalled in [0, P ), and that tasks in the busy interval start executing at the beginning of a regulation interval at time t = P . Finally, we add a term MD i,p (t) to represent the maximum delay caused to the i-level busy interval in [P, t) due to either regulation or interference. div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: We evaluate our proposed server by generating interfaces for tasks on M = 2, 4 or 8 cores and testing schedulability using the system-level analysis based on the memory delay formulation in [38]. Since we are interested in understanding the improvements in terms of task set schedulability achievable by our technique, and not in validating the underlying memory delay analyses, we base our evaluation on synthetic task generation. As stressed in Section III, we assume that main memory is the only source of inter-core interference and ignore all other physical shared resources in the system. We refer the interested reader to [38], [16] for evaluation of the underlying analyses and more in-depth discussion of the corresponding models and limitations.

We provide results for five cases. In the figures, 'unreg' represents an unregulated system where the number of requests of competing cores is unknown; hence, only request driven analysis can be used. 'non-comp' again represents an unregulated system, but using the best bound between the request and job driven analysis. This approach is non-compositional, since it requires simultaneous knowledge of all tasks' parameters in the system. 'read-reg' and 'rw-reg' are the discussed memory server analyses for the case of read regulation and read/write regulation, respectively. Finally, 'legacy' represents a regulation approach similar to [18]. Under this approach, read/write regulation is used similarly to rw-reg, but rather than assigning a different memory budget to each server, all servers use the same memory budget Q. The budget Q is determined by first computing the minimum guaranteed bandwidth provided by the memory controller, which can be obtained assuming that successive memory requests all target different rows in the same DRAM bank, and then splitting such bandwidth equally among the M cores. Schedulability is then determined by checking whether the budget assignment Q p = Q, QB p = (M -1) • Q falls within the schedulability envelope of each core. Finally, note that we do not compare against the method in [12] because it relies on request driven bounds only; therefore, its per-core schedulability cannot be better than unreg, which we use as a baseline. All results are based on a LPDDR2 533Mhz memory as discussed in Section II-C. Unless otherwise stated, we use a regulation period P = 1ms.

Synthetic tasks are generated as follows. Given a percore utilization U and number of tasks per core N , we first generate uniform task utilizations u 1,p , . . . , u N,p such that i=1...N u i,p = U . We then extract the period T i,p for each task according to a uniform distribution in [10, 1000]ms, and set C i,p = T i,p • u i,p . Deadline is set equal to period. The total number of memory requests H R i,p and H W i,p is determined based on C i,p and the task's randomly generated bandwidth requirement B i,p . B i,p represents the percentage of time that the task is accessing main memory: for B i,p = 100%, the task continuously generates requests at the maximum rate sustainable by memory of one request every tBU RST = 4 memory cycles. To vary the memory intensiveness of the task set, for each experiment we pick a value B max and uniformly extract B i,p in interval [0, B max ]. To split the computed total number of memory requests between H R i,p and H W i,p , we then randomly determine the percentage of write requests for the task according to a uniform distribution between 10% and 40%, which are realistic ranges for real benchmarks [15]. For each utilization point, we generate 1000 task sets and evaluate their schedulability according to the five aforementioned schemes; the employed code is available at [23].

Figure 2 shows results in terms of average number of schedulable task sets as a function of the per-core utilization U , for M = 4, N = 10 7 and task bandwidth B max = 1%. Note that despite the low amount of required memory bandwidth, unreg exhibits a significant drop in schedulable utilization, while non-comp has the best schedulability; this is not surprising, since request driven analysis results in large delay bounds for unregulated FR-FCFS arbitration, while the non-compositional case can best use job driven analysis, having a complete view of tasks' parameters on all cores. For the memory server, read/write regulation performs better than read regulation only; as noted in Section IV-D, this is because read/write regulation suffers significantly less contention from other cores compared to read regulation. Finally, legacy performs only slightly better than unreg.

Since all graphs in Figure 2 show sharp thresholds, in the next set of Figures 345we instead vary B max and plot the utilization at which a given graph reaches the threshold of 50% schedulable task sets for that B max value. In Figures 34we vary B max in the (0, 10)% range, which is realistic for most benchmark, and use either M = 2 or 8 cores. The general trend is similar to Figure 2, with the exception of legacy. For low values of B max , legacy performs the same as unreg, since the assigned per-core budget Q ends up being too large to take advantage of the job driven bounds. As the value of B max increases, the total amount of request driven delay increases since the busy interval under analysis generates more requests. However, the job driven delay depends only on the budget assigned to other cores, which is constant for legacy: hence, at some point the job driven delay becomes smaller than the request driven delay and legacy improves over unreg. Also note that for a given B max value, the schedulable utilization for non-comp, rw-reg and legacy decreases as M increases, since more cores result in additional interference for job driven analysis. Figure 5 depicts threshold utilization results for M = 4, except that B max is varied in (0, 100)%. While such settings for B max are not fully realistic, they nevertheless help to explain the behaviour of the analyses for high task bandwidth values. Note that rw-reg always performs at least as good as legacy, since the same delay analysis is applied in both cases, but rw-reg has the flexibility to assign different budgets to cores. For a similar reason, at high B max values, regulation approaches tends to perform better than the unregulated, non-compositional approach: the amount of budget assigned to some cores can be restricted in order to 7 While we performed experiments with varying number of tasks, the value of N does not appear to significantly affect the schedulability results. Finally, in Figures 6,7 we evaluate the effects of changing the regulation period P by plotting the schedulable utilization for a system with M = 4 and either B max = 0.5% or 8%. Note that the curves for unreg and non-comp are constant, since they do not use regulation. rw-reg and read-reg reach zero schedulable utilization for values of P above 10ms, which is expected since the minimum task period is 10ms, but are otherwise little affected by the choice of P . On the other hand, legacy is highly affected by the value of the regulation period, for a similar reason as noted before: when the value of P is small, the assigned per-core budget Q is too large and legacy behaves as unreg; when the value of P is large, the budget Q is too small and the cores are excessively delayed due to regulation. For values in between, legacy comes close to read-reg but is always below rw-reg, as in Figures 345. However, note that the best regulation period assignment for legacy varies widely between Figure 6 and7: this shows that a constant per-core bandwidth assignment is not capable of adapting to different tasks' bandwidth requirements.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Managing shared physical resources efficiently is of paramount importance in multicore real-time systems. COTS memory controllers pose special challenges, since their em-ployed arbitration schemes make the derivation of tight delay bounds particularly difficult. In this paper, we have proposed the abstraction of a memory server for partitioned multicore systems. By tightly controlling the allocation of memory bandwidth and separating the derivation of the schedulability interface for each core from the system-level analysis, our proposed solution supports independent subsystem development without unduly impacting system schedulability.

As future work, we plan to study how to apply our proposed technique to other physical resources. As discussed in the paper, we believe that our server can be useful not just for main memory, but for any physical resource and associated analysis which produces tighter job driven bounds compared to request driven bounds. For example, it is known that request driven bounds for network-on-chips with wormhole routing and virtual channels are extremely pessimistic: even with round-robin arbitration, the worst case contention suffered by a flit is proportional to the number of ports per switch times the number of virtual channels times the number of hops, which is much larger than the actual number of cores. We expect that regulating NoC accesses similarly to a memory server could lead to reasonable delay bounds without resorting to non-compositional analysis [31]. We also plan to extend our method to allow multiple servers to coexist on the same core, similarly to the Multi-Resource Server detailed in [21], [12].

In details, following Sections IV-B -IV-D, we show how to compute the contention delay MD int i,p (t) and how to derive the server interface for both read and read/write regulation.
